steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Skylights and caves on Mars and the Moon could give us astrobiological samples, answer questions about geological origins, and show a subsurface world that has not been discovered yet. These environments clearly have scientific value, but exploring them is a daunting technical challenge. Navigating perilous, unknown terrain needs an innovative solution that can move in a versatile way through loose material and around unpredictable obstacles. ReachBot is a robot concept that answers this call for mobility in extreme environments.

As discussed in previous work, the limbs of ReachBot are extendable booms that act as prismatic joints, so it has a large workspace compared to traditional rigid-link designs. These booms are steerable, and when they are paired with grippers ReachBot can climb and span steep verticals inside caverns where a jumping robot or aerial robot may not be able to go, as shown in Fig. 1 (A,B). The booms could also be combined with other technologies like cables or tethers, as shown in Fig. 1 (C), to increase reach further and reduce mass and volume complexity. Because ReachBot has a large workspace, more anchor points in the environment are reachable, and this is especially useful in unknown environments where anchor points are sparse or the terrain has obstructions.

The gripper at the end of each boom has microspines to grasp the environment. Microspines have been used in many works to grasp rough and rocky surfaces, including for planetary exploration, and the conditions for successful grasping with microspines have been analyzed in several works. As shown in Fig. 1 (B), the ReachBot gripper can successfully grasp surface locations that are approximately convex.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Skylights and caves on Mars and the Moon could give us astrobiological samples, answer questions about geological origins, and show a subsurface world that has not been discovered yet. These environments clearly have scientific value, but exploring them is a daunting technical challenge. Navigating perilous, unknown terrain needs an innovative solution that can move in a versatile way through loose material and around unpredictable obstacles. ReachBot is a robot concept that answers this call for mobility in extreme environments.

As discussed in previous work, the limbs of ReachBot are extendable booms that act as prismatic joints, so it has a large workspace compared to traditional rigid-link designs. These booms are steerable, and when they are paired with grippers ReachBot can climb and span steep verticals inside caverns where a jumping robot or aerial robot may not be able to go, as shown in Fig. 1 (A,B). The booms could also be combined with other technologies like cables or tethers, as shown in Fig. 1 (C), to increase reach further and reduce mass and volume complexity. Because ReachBot has a large workspace, more anchor points in the environment are reachable, and this is especially useful in unknown environments where anchor points are sparse or the terrain has obstructions.

The gripper at the end of each boom has microspines to grasp the environment. Microspines have been used in many works to grasp rough and rocky surfaces, including for planetary exploration, and the conditions for successful grasping with microspines have been analyzed in several works. As shown in Fig. 1 (B), the ReachBot gripper can successfully grasp surface locations that are approximately convex.

ReachBot's mechanical architecture and motion planning have been studied before, but there has been comparatively scant analysis of the perception system trade space. Early indoor work assumed the grasping locations were known, captured by overhead cameras. Later a two-stage perception strategy and sensor system was introduced and demonstrated successfully in field testing in a Mojave Desert lava tube, but it only used RGB-D images in daylight and did not review other sensing modalities or mission-level considerations. RGB-D images work in the field, but alternatives should be investigated for more realistic mission conditions. Any perception system that operates in caves and skylights has to face the typical subsurface concerns, which are low power, limited communication bandwidth, total darkness, and dusty conditions. On top of these, and making them worse, there are the operational challenges of any space hardware: radiation hardening, thermal requirements, mass/volume restrictions, cost, and technological risk. Also, since ReachBot has a much larger workspace than a typical climbing robot, high-level sensing strategies should be examined too.

## Statement of Contributions

In this work we evaluate the perception system approaches that let ReachBot identify grasping sites. We build on the previous ReachBot analysis and also on existing work for subsurface robots that use distance-based sensing. Our main contributions are:

- 1. We present a survey of different robotic sensing modalities for a climbing robot in a subsurface environment.

- 2. We discuss perception system strategies and candidate map outputs for a ReachBot perception system.

- 3. We propose evaluation criteria for sensor hardware, for a configuration of ReachBot that discerns grasping locations in a martian lava tube environment.

- 4. We conduct trades and propose a hardware configuration that could be physically prototyped and tested in a lava tube test environment.

## Paper Organization

The rest of the paper is organized like this. In Section II we describe background literature on the perception systems of robots that are designed either for climbing with microspines or for subsurface exploration. We also discuss considerations for upstream trades about the choice of perception strategy, and downstream trades about the choice of environment representation for the planner. Section III discusses the trade study process. Then in Section IV we develop evaluation criteria for sensor selection, and in Section V we present the viable perception architectures for a specific ReachBot mission. After that we analyze the different map representation choices in Section VI. Finally we give conclusions and suggest next steps for this work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Skylights and caves on Mars and the Moon could yield astrobiological samples, unlock answers about geological origins, and reveal a previously undiscovered subsurface world. While such environments have clear scientific value, exploring them is a daunting technical challenge: navigating perilous, unknown terrain requires an innovative solution capable of versatile mobility through loose material and unpredictable obstacles. ReachBot is a robot concept that answers this call for mobility in extreme environments.

As discussed in previous work [1,2,3,4,5], ReachBot's limbs are extendable booms that act as prismatic joints, achieving a large workspace compared to traditional rigid-link designs. When paired with grippers, these steerable booms enable ReachBot to climb and span steep verticals inside caverns that a jumping robot or aerial robot may fail to access, as shown in Fig. 1 (A,B). The booms could also be combined with other technologies, such as cables or tethers as shown in Fig. 1 (C), to further increase reach and reduce mass and volume complexity. ReachBot's large workspace expands the number of reachable anchor points in the environment, which is especially advantageous in unknown environments with sparse anchor points or obstructions in terrain.

To grasp the environment, the gripper at the end of each boom is equipped with microspines. Microspines have been used in multiple works to grasp rough and rocky surfaces, including for planetary exploration [6,7,8,9,10], and several works have analyzed the conditions for successful grasping with microspines [11,8,12]. As shown in Fig. 1 (B), the ReachBot gripper successfully grasps surface locations that are approximately convex.

While ReachBot's mechanical architecture and motion planning have been studied before, analysis of the perception system trade space has been comparatively scant. Early indoor work assumed known grasping locations captured by overhead cameras [2]. Later, a two-stage perception strategy and sensor system was introduced in a successful field testing demonstration in a Mojave Desert lava tube [13], but this used only RGB-D images in daylight and did not review other sensing modalities or mission-level considerations. Although RGB-D images work in the field, alternatives should be investigated for more realistic mission conditions. To operate in caves and skylights, every perception system must face the typical subsurface concerns: low power, limited communication bandwidth, total darkness, and dusty conditions. These are compounded by the operational challenges of any space hardware, namely radiation hardening, thermal requirements, mass/volume restrictions, cost, and technological risk. Because ReachBot's workspace is much larger than that of a typical climbing robot, an examination of high-level sensing strategies is also warranted.

## I- 1 Statement of Contributions

This work evaluates the perception system approaches that enable ReachBot to identify grasping sites, building on previous ReachBot analysis as well as existing work for subsurface robots that use distance-based sensing. The main contributions of this work are:

- 1. We present a survey of different robotic sensing modalities for a climbing robot in a subsurface environment.

- 2. We discuss perception system strategies and candidate map outputs of a ReachBot perception system.

- 3. We propose evaluation criteria for sensor hardware for a configuration of ReachBot that discerns grasping locations in a martian lava tube environment.

- 4. We conduct trades and propose a hardware configuration that could be physically prototyped for testing in a lava tube test environment.

## I- 2 Paper Organization

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes background literature on the perception systems of robots designed either for climbing with microspines or for subsurface exploration, and discusses considerations for upstream trades around the choice of perception strategy and downstream trades on the choice of environment representation for the planner. Section III discusses the trade study process. We then develop evaluation criteria for sensor selection in Section IV and present the viable perception architectures for a specific ReachBot mission in Section V. Section VI analyzes the different map representation choices. Finally, we provide conclusions and suggest next steps for this work.
